settings.name: Vera’s Flat (Old Town)
settings.description: A cramped apartment above a printer’s shop, smelling of wet ink and stale tobacco, with peeling wallpaper that mirrors the crumbling political facade.

settings.name: Ministry of Culture
settings.description: A brutalist concrete building near Wenceslas Square, echoing with the hollow clatter of typewriters and the damp chill of unheated corridors.

settings.name: The Café Louvre
settings.description: A historic café where Jiri meets Vera, smelling of roasted beans and old wood, a space of relative warmth before the cold sets in.

settings.name: Karlovy Vary Train Station
settings.description: A transit hub of steam and confusion, smelling of coal dust and fear, where travelers move like ghosts in the fog.

settings.name: The Border Checkpoint (Cheb)
settings.description: A stark military outpost smelling of diesel and rain, dominated by the glare of floodlights and the rigid posture of soldiers.

plot_points.description: Vera translates a innocuous poem for Jiri, unaware it contains coded references to the satchel’s contents.
Jiri hands Vera the leather satchel, warning her that paper is heavier than lead; she hides it under floorboards.
The tanks arrive; Vera watches from her window as the sky turns grey with smoke, realizing her translation work is now treason.
The Ministry purges its staff; Vera is suspended not for the manuscript, but for her "Western associations," isolating her completely.
Colonel Hanzl visits Vera’s mother, not demanding the book, but asking about Vera’s loneliness, implying he holds the power to make her life unbearable or empty.

At the border checkpoint, Vera must decide whether to burn the manuscript to prove her innocence or carry it and risk execution; she chooses to carry it, but Lukas is caught with a duplicate, revealing her route.
(resolution, ch15) Vera escapes into the woods, leaving the satchel behind to save herself, keeping only a single page in her pocket, a fragment of the whole.

themes: The ethics of preservation versus survival
the erosion of trust in bureaucratic language
voice: Close third-person, past tense, restrained and atmospheric, focusing on the tactile reality of objects and the chilling silence of occupied spaces.
